newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs level Moslem homes after UN lists owners.
newsitem.headline: Serbs level Moslem homes after UN lists owners.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities blew up 96 Moslem homes after the U.N. provided a list of their refugee owners who had applied to visit the properties, U.N. officials said on Wednesday.
"The Serbs simply matched the 96 names to 96 abandoned homes and demolished the homes," said Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Bosnia.

"What is so discouraging is that our effort to bring people back together again was used to cement (wartime) ethnic cleansing by destroying the property of people who might want to return," he said at a news briefing.
The 96 homes were blown up on October 24 in the Prijedor area of Bosnia's Serb Republic.

Anti-tank mines were used to flatten the houses in an operation so swift and professional that it must have been sponsored or carried out by local paramilitary police, U.N. and NATO peace force sources said.

Under the 1995 Dayton peace treaty signed by Moslem, Serb and Croat factions, hundreds of thousands of war refugees were to be allowed to cross entity boundary lines to visit and ultimately reclaim their homes.
But nationalist factions have barred all but a few refugees from returning and many empty homes in the Serb entity, and to a lesser extent in the Moslem-Croat Federation, have been torched.
Janowski said the UNHCR set up a programme for returning war refugees early this year but only one in 10 of the visits organised to date had been carried out.

In mid-October, 96 Moslem refugees now living in the Federation-controlled northwestern town of Sanski Most applied through the UNHCR to revisit their old homes in the Prijedor area, 30 km (18 miles) to the north.

"The normal procedure is to give a list of people intending to visit their homes to the authorities of the receiving entity," Janowski said. "In this case we gave the list to the (Serb) mayor of Prijedor.

"It was a list of people, not houses. But it was apparently turned from a visit list into a demolition list. However, leaders of the (Moslem) displaced have told us they still want to have a look even though the houses were blown up."

Janowski said the Prijedor mayor must have passed the list to his police force, notorious for its involvement in mass expulsions of Moslems during the war and its defiance of the peace implementation process since then.

Last week, international peace coordinators discovered that four policemen on the Prijedor force were indicted war criminals sought by the international tribunal on former Yugoslavia, based in The Hague.

Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic promised to sack the four after demarches by peace officials and John Shattuck, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for human rights. But she refused to surrender them to the tribunal.
